meta.objective: Can we describe, explain and forecast the number of bikes rented per day in Washington DC from the weather and the calendar?

units.title: Introduction to Data Science
units.stage: Prior knowledge → Preparation (and how models are validated)
units.paragraph: The objective was to describe, explain and forecast the number of bikes rented per day from the weather and the calendar. The raw file has 731 days and 16 columns (2011-01-01 to 2012-12-31). Cleaning found 0 duplicates, no missing values and one invalid value: humidity 0 % on 2011-03-10, replaced by 71.2 %, the mean of the two neighbouring days. The weather columns were de-normalised to °C, % and km/h, and the days were split in time order into 547 training days and 184 test days. On the simplest model, rentals = 1,054.57 + 149.01 × temperature, the hold-out gave a training MAE of 1,046 rentals but a test MAE of 1,924; 5-fold cross-validation averaged 1,405, and 200 bootstrap samples put the slope between 137.01 and 160.18 rentals per °C.
units.one_line: The test error (1,924) is far above the training error (1,046): rentals grew in 2012, so a line fitted on the past under-predicts the future.

units.title: Data exploration using descriptive statistics
units.paragraph: From one frequency table of 11 classes of width 800, the step-deviation method gives a mean of 4,507 rentals per day, a median of 4,498 and a mode of 4,443, so Mode < Median < Mean. Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness is 0.03 and Bowley's is 0.04: both are close to 0, so the distribution is nearly symmetric. The standard deviation is 1,944 rentals, and β₂ = 2.23 < 3, so the curve is platykurtic (flatter than normal). Rentals average 4,877 on clear days, 4,036 on misty days and 1,803 on rainy or snowy days. Karl Pearson's r between temperature and rentals is 0.6275 (a moderate degree positive correlation); humidity (-0.1159) and wind speed (-0.2345) are low-degree negative.
units.one_line: Rentals are symmetric around 4,507 per day, and temperature is the one weather variable with a sizeable correlation (r = 0.63).

units.title: Data exploration using inferential statistics
units.paragraph: Treating the 731 days as a sample, a 95 % confidence interval from 50 random days puts the mean daily rentals between 3,766 and 4,840. The Z-test of the 2012 mean (5,600) against the 2011 mean (3,406) gives Z = 23.47, far beyond the tabulated 1.96, so H₀ is rejected: demand really rose. The paired t-test on the same 12 calendar months agrees (t = -12.85). Two tests accept H₀: the 21 holidays are not significantly different from the overall mean (t = -1.68 vs 2.086), and working days do not differ from non-working days (t = 0.41 vs 2.013). One-way ANOVA by season gives F = 128.78 against a 5 % limit of 2.62: the season means (Winter 2,604, Spring 4,992, Summer 5,644, Fall 4,728) are significantly different. The two-way ANOVA on year × quarter rejects both: F = 188.5 for the year effect and F = 60.4 for the quarter effect.
units.one_line: Year and season matter (both rejected at 5 %); the day of the week and holidays do not (both accepted).

units.title: Regression analysis
units.paragraph: The simple regression Y = 1,054.57 + 149.01 X says each extra °C adds about 149 rentals, and it explains R² = 0.42 of the daily variation on the training days. Adding humidity as a second predictor gives Ŷ = 2,686.06 + 157.21 X₁ − 28.68 X₂ with R² = 0.48: holding humidity constant each °C adds 157 rentals, and holding temperature constant each 1 % of humidity removes 29. The partial coefficient of humidity is much larger than its simple slope because temperature and humidity are nearly unrelated (r₁₂ = 0.14). The F-test rejects H₀ (F = 251.0 vs 3.01) and both t-tests reject it (t₁ = 21.88, t₂ = -7.95 vs 1.964), so the model and each coefficient are significant. Adding wind and the year indicator (Design C: temp + hum + wind + yr) lifts R² to 0.74: the year dummy alone is worth about 1,791 rentals per day, and the test-period MAE falls from 1,943 to 1,126.

numbers.label: Best design R², test MAE
numbers.hint: Design C: temp + hum + wind + yr

units.one_line: Weather alone explains about half the daily variation (R² = 0.48); the year effect (+1,791 rentals) is the single biggest term.

units.title: Anomaly detection
units.paragraph: On rentals alone the statistical rules find nothing: the |z| > 3 rule flags 0 days and the 1.5 × IQR rule flags 0, because the distribution is wide. Even Hurricane Sandy, the lowest day in the data, has z = -2.31. The same rule does find 2 wind-speed outliers and 2 days on the raw humidity column (the 0 % sensor error among them). Looking at two variables together changes the picture: on standardised (temperature, rentals) the k-NN distance ranks Sandy 3rd of 731 days and the local outlier factor gives it LOF = 1.95 (rank 4); the top day by both methods is 2011-08-27 (Hurricane Irene passes Washington DC, LOF = 2.58). For the supervised case, high-demand days (more than 7,000 rentals) are 27 of 547 training days, about 1 : 19. SMOTE raises the minority class to 520 by adding 493 synthetic days; logistic regression then finds 91.0 % of the test high-demand days instead of 4.5 %, while precision moves from 20.0 % to 57.6 % and F1 from 0.07 to 0.71.
units.one_line: One-variable rules miss the storm days; distance and density methods on two variables catch them, and SMOTE makes the rare high-demand class learnable.

units.title: Time series forecasting
units.paragraph: The monthly series rises from 1,232 rentals per day in Jan 2011 to a peak of 7,286 in Sep 2012: a strong upward trend with a yearly seasonal swing. On the 8 quarterly means the additive decomposition fits better, because the seasonal swing grew only 6.5 % while the level grew 64.7 %; it forecasts 2013 Q1–Q4 at 6,242, 8,558, 8,918 and 7,910 rentals per day. Forecasting the 6 test months from the 18 training months, the average method is worst (MAE 1,926, MASE 3.46) because old low months never leave the mean; the moving average (k = 3) is best (MAE 958, MAPE 19.5 %, MASE 1.72) because it follows the level just reached. Regression on time (slope 210.78 rentals per month, MAE 1,196) and ARIMA(1, 1, 0) (MAE 1,245) keep the growth going but have no seasonal term, so they miss the autumn turn. Every MASE is above 1: none of the methods beat the one-step naive forecast on these months.
units.one_line: Demand is growing about 211 rentals per day each month with a summer peak; short memory (moving average (k = 3)) forecasts it best.

actions.finding: Temperature is the strongest weather driver: r = 0.63 (Unit 2); holding humidity constant each 1 °C adds 157 rentals, and each 1 % of humidity removes 29 (Unit 4).
actions.action: Put more bikes on the street on warm, dry days and fewer on cold or humid ones; use the two-predictor equation with the day's forecast temperature and humidity to size the fleet.

actions.finding: Seasons differ significantly (F = 128.8 vs 2.62, Unit 3): Winter averages 2,604 rentals per day, Summer 5,644. High-demand days (more than 7,000 rentals) are 94 of 731 days (12.9 %) overall, 23.9 % of summer days and 0.5 % of winter days.
actions.action: Plan the summer roster for about one high-demand day in 4; schedule maintenance and rebalancing crews in winter, when demand is roughly half the yearly mean.

actions.finding: Working days and non-working days do not differ (t = 0.41 vs 2.013, H₀ accepted), nor do holidays (t = -1.68 vs 2.086).
actions.action: Do not run a separate weekend or holiday fleet plan; the weather and the season decide the day, not the calendar.

actions.finding: Storm days are the real outliers: 2012-10-29 (Hurricane Sandy, 22 rentals) and 2011-08-27 (Hurricane Irene, LOF = 2.58). One-variable rules flag 0 of them; the two-variable k-NN and LOF methods rank them at the top.
actions.action: Monitor rentals together with temperature, not rentals alone; a warm day with almost no rentals is a system or weather emergency. Pull bikes off the street when a storm is forecast and expect near-zero revenue that day.

actions.finding: Demand grew from 3,406 rentals per day in 2011 to 5,600 in 2012 (Z = 23.5, Unit 3); the year indicator is worth about 1,791 rentals per day in the regression (Unit 4), and the additive decomposition forecasts 8,918 per day for 2013 Q3 (Unit 6).
actions.action: Budget the next year's fleet and docks for growth, not for the current level: the summer peak of the next year will be above anything seen so far.

actions.finding: Among the forecasting methods, moving average (k = 3) had the lowest test error (MAE 958, MASE 1.72); the average method was worst (MAE 1,926, MASE 3.46).
actions.action: For month-ahead planning use the last three months, re-forecast every month, and never use the long-run average while the trend is this steep.

actions.finding: With SMOTE the classifier finds 91.0 % of high-demand test days instead of 4.5 %, at the cost of 45 false alarms instead of 12 (Unit 5).
actions.action: Use the balanced classifier as an early-warning flag for high-demand days: a missed busy day costs more than an unnecessary extra shift.

actions.finding: The hold-out test error (1,924) is almost twice the training error (1,046) because the series grows (Unit 1).
actions.action: Always validate on a later period than the one the model was fitted on; a random split would hide the growth and overstate accuracy.

limitations.title: Two years only
limitations.detail: The data cover 2011-01-01 to 2012-12-31: 24 monthly points and 8 quarters. One year of growth cannot tell whether the trend continues, flattens or was special to 2012.

limitations.title: Weather explains about half of the daily variation
limitations.detail: The two-predictor model reaches R² = 0.48; only when the year indicator is added does R² reach 0.74. The rest is events, marketing, the growth of the system and the day-to-day noise of people's plans.

limitations.title: Monthly forecasts without a seasonal term miss the autumn turn
limitations.detail: Regression on t and ARIMA(1, 1, 0) keep rising after September; the best method (Moving average (k = 3)) still has MASE = 1.72 > 1, so none of them beats a one-step naive forecast on the six test months. A seasonal model needs more than two years to estimate its indices.

limitations.title: SMOTE interpolates 0/1 columns
limitations.detail: Synthetic days are drawn on the straight line between two real high-demand days, so the 0/1 columns working-day and year become fractions between 0 and 1; the classifier treats them as numbers, which is acceptable for logistic regression but is not a real calendar.

limitations.title: Correlation, not causation
limitations.detail: Weather can affect rentals but rentals cannot affect the weather, so the direction is clear; the year effect, however, bundles everything that changed between 2011 and 2012 (more docks, more members, more publicity) into one number.

course_conclusion: This project walked through the complete data science workflow — data acquisition, preparation, exploration, modelling and evaluation — on one dataset, using the statistical techniques, regression, anomaly detection and time series forecasting methods of the course exactly as they were taught, so that every number on every page can be traced back to a formula from class and a line of code that computed it.
